raw_findings.message: The handler trusts an arbitrary Content-Length and reads that many bytes without a limit, allowing a client to consume excessive memory or tie up a request thread with a large or incomplete body.
Unhandled exceptions are returned with full tracebacks, exposing internal paths and implementation details to any caller who triggers an error.
The connection acquired before parsing the request is not released when malformed JSON or an invalid date causes an early return, so repeated requests can exhaust database connections.
Expense ownership is taken directly from the caller-controlled X-User header, allowing a caller to create expenses as another user; the budget endpoint likewise trusts a caller-supplied user field.
Read endpoints use the caller-supplied user query parameter without checking authorization, allowing anyone to retrieve another user's expenses, summaries, and reports.
The user query parameter is interpolated into SQL, so a crafted value such as an injected tautology can expose expenses belonging to every user.
A summary for a user and month with no expenses passes zero active days to daily_average and raises an exception instead of returning an empty summary.
User-controlled category and note values are written into CSV cells without neutralizing spreadsheet formula prefixes, so opening a generated report can execute attacker-supplied formulas.
The export path is joined without validating or constraining the supplied name, allowing an unauthenticated caller to use an absolute path or ../ segments to read arbitrary files.
The admin token is embedded in source code, so anyone who can read the project can authenticate to the admin stats endpoint with this known credential.
daily_average divides by days without handling zero, which makes summaries for periods with no expenses fail.
subcategory indexes the second split component without checking that a category contains a colon, so an accepted category such as "food" makes summary requests fail.

fixed_raw_findings.message: The handler trusts an arbitrary Content-Length and reads that many bytes, so a client can send an excessively large body or keep a thread blocked while it waits for the declared body.
Connections are released only on the success path, so a SQLite error such as binding an out-of-range integer leaves a connection open and repeated requests can exhaust resources.
set_budget trusts the user supplied in the request body without checking it against X-User, allowing a caller to change another user's budget.
create_report does not verify the requested user against X-User, so a caller can generate a report containing another user's expense data and retrieve it through the export endpoint.

The user and month values are interpolated into a filename without path validation, so slash and .. components can make the report write escape REPORTS_DIR and overwrite a file accessible to the service.
User-controlled category and note values are written as unescaped CSV cells, so a value beginning with a spreadsheet formula can execute when the report is opened in spreadsheet software.
int() silently truncates JSON floats, so a request with amount_cents set to a positive fractional value is accepted as a smaller integer amount.

raw_findings.message: Returning full tracebacks to clients exposes filesystem paths, SQL details, and other internal implementation information when a handler raises an exception.
Malformed JSON returns without releasing the connection acquired at line 93, so repeated invalid requests accumulate open database connections; the invalid-day branch has the same leak.
Any caller can choose another user's X-User value and create expenses under that identity because the header is trusted without authentication or authorization.
Any caller can supply another user's name in the query and retrieve that user's expenses because the endpoint performs no authorization check.
The user query parameter is interpolated directly into SQL, so a crafted value such as `' OR 1=1 --` can return expenses belonging to every user.
The request body selects the budget owner without checking the caller's identity, allowing anyone to overwrite another user's budget.
User-controlled category and note fields are written into CSV without escaping or formula neutralization, so spreadsheet users can trigger formula execution by opening a crafted report.
The caller-controlled path is joined to the reports directory without containment checks, so an absolute path or `../` traversal can make the server return arbitrary readable files.
The admin token is embedded in source code, allowing anyone who can obtain the project code to authenticate to the admin statistics endpoint.
A summary with no matching expenses passes zero active days here and raises instead of returning an empty-period result.
A category without a colon raises IndexError when summarized, so an ordinary expense category can make the summary endpoint fail.

The self-check compares the query parameter with the caller-controlled X-User header, so a client can set both to a victim's name and read that user's expenses and summary.
If a database operation after acquire raises an exception, such as SQLite rejecting an oversized integer amount, the handler skips release and repeated requests retain connections indefinitely.
The budget endpoint accepts a user from the request body without checking the caller, so anyone can create or replace another user's budget.
